summary: Introduces a MIB module defining textual conventions for commonly used transport-layer addresses. The definitions fit the TAddress and TDomain approach from SMIv2 and support Internet transport protocols over both IPv4 and IPv6, so other MIB modules can reuse them.

eli5.summary: When many forms ask for an address, it helps if they all use the same box layout. This note defines standard address boxes for network-management data.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
how is an ipv6 address and port encoded in a mib
subtitle: A shared MIB module that gives network-management data standard ways to write down a transport address such as an IP address plus port.

tldr.problem: Many MIB modules need to hold a transport-layer address, but the existing TDomain and TAddress definitions were mixed with SNMP semantics and had nothing for Internet transports over IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The TRANSPORT-ADDRESS-MIB module defines TransportDomain, TransportAddressType and TransportAddress, 16 registered transport domains, and address formats for IPv4, IPv6, zone indexes, POSIX local IPC and DNS names.
tldr.outcome: MIB authors get one set of reusable definitions. The module defines no managed objects of its own, and the RFC says it has no impact on Internet security.

today: RFC 3419 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of these conventions as published. It builds on RFC 2579 and sits beside RFC 3417.

sections.title: Why Transport Address Conventions
sections.content:
Several MIB modules need to represent transport-layer addresses in a generic way. Typical cases are MIBs for application protocols that can run over several transports, and MIBs that model generic communication endpoints.

SMIv2 (RFC 2579) already defines TDomain and TAddress. A TAddress value is interpreted in the transport domain named by a TDomain, which is an object identifier so that authors can add their own domains. The initial set was standardized in RFC 3417, but those definitions are mixed up with SNMP semantics and have none for Internet transports over IPv4 and IPv6.

This memo adds well-known textual conventions that stay compatible with the TDomain and TAddress approach, covers more Internet transports over IPv4 and IPv6, and adds an enumeration of the well-known domains. An enumeration can be more efficient than an object identifier.
sections.eli5: Network-management files needed a standard way to write 'this address, on this kind of connection'. The old way was tied to one use and missed newer address types.

sections.title: What the Module Defines
sections.content:
The module provides four kinds of definitions: generic TransportAddress and TransportDomain conventions, object identifier registrations for well-known transport domains, an enumeration of those domains called TransportAddressType, and concrete address-format conventions whose DISPLAY-HINTs are aligned with the formats used in URIs.

New domains can be added in two ways. The module itself can be updated with new constants for both TransportDomain and TransportAddressType, or another MIB module can define its own domain and conventions. The second route cannot extend the TransportAddressType enumeration. So a designer chooses between the compact TransportAddressType with limited extensibility and the more verbose TransportDomain that allows arbitrary extension.

The module does not define the transport mappings of any particular protocol. It supplies common identifiers and conventions for transport mapping documents to use.
sections.eli5: It gives you a short list of ready-made kinds of connection with numbers. If you need a kind that is not on the list, you can make your own, but then you give up the short numbered list.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
A TAddress is an octet string of 1 to 255 octets. Experience showed a need to represent unknown addresses, so TransportAddress allows 0 to 255 octets. Constrained to SIZE (1..255) it is identical to TAddress. New MIB modules SHOULD use TransportDomain, TransportAddressType and TransportAddress, and existing ones can swap in TransportDomain for TDomain.

The SNMPv2-TM domains from RFC 3417 all have snmp in their names and were meant for SNMP only, although they were later used for other endpoints. The domains in this memo are independent of the protocol on top and SHOULD be used for all endpoints that do not carry SNMP traffic. Endpoints that do carry SNMP SHOULD keep using SNMPv2-TM where it applies, and use this memo's domains for cases it lacks, such as SNMP over UDP over IPv6. Programs that interpret domain values should accept both sets.

The INET-ADDRESS-MIB conventions from RFC 3291, with InetPortNumber, suit MIBs specific to Internet transports. For protocols that may use other transports, this memo's definitions are more appropriate.
sections.eli5: Older address boxes are still fine for the jobs they were made for. The new boxes are for everything else, and programs should understand both.

sections.title: Domains and Address Formats
sections.content:
The module registers 16 transport domains under transportDomains. They combine UDP, TCP or SCTP with IPv4, IPv6, or a DNS name, plus a POSIX local IPC domain. For IPv4 and IPv6 there are plain forms and scoped forms with a zone index, marked with a z. The enumerated TransportAddressType values equal the last sub-identifier of the matching object identifier, with unknown(0) added.

Each domain pairs with an address convention. TransportAddressIPv4 is 6 octets (4 for the address, 2 for the port). TransportAddressIPv6 is 18 octets. The z forms insert a zone index: TransportAddressIPv4z is 10 octets and TransportAddressIPv6z is 22 octets. All numbers are in network byte order. TransportAddressLocal holds a POSIX local IPC address, which subsumes UNIX domain sockets. TransportAddressDns holds a DNS name, a colon and a port number written in ASCII.

The specific conventions SHOULD NOT be used directly in object definitions, since they fix one format. DNS values need run-time resolution, so any object that may hold one must fully describe how and when names are resolved.
sections.eli5: Each kind of address has a fixed box layout, like street, then door number. The DNS version is different: it just writes a name and a number and leaves the lookup for later.

sections.title: Rules for Using TransportAddress
sections.content:
A TransportAddress value is always interpreted in the context of a TransportAddressType or TransportDomain object. Every use MUST say which object provides that context, and MIB authors SHOULD define a separate domain or type object for each address object. The value must be consistent with that object. An attempt to set an inconsistent value must fail with an inconsistentValue error.

When the convention is used as an index, the SMIv2 limit of 128 sub-identifiers can be a problem. The OBJECT-TYPE declaration then MUST include a SIZE clause to bound the instance sub-identifiers. For scoped addresses, authors SHOULD use a separate domain or type object for each address object, so combinations of scoped addresses stay unambiguous.
sections.eli5: An address on its own is meaningless. You always have to say what kind of address it is, and the two must match.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven examples showing the hex encoding and the rendered display. A global IPv4 address on port 80 is encoded as 86A922010050 and shows as 134.169.34.1:80. The IPv6 forms are shown in brackets, as in [1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A]:80.

A link-local IPv6 address with zone index 42 on port 80 shows as [FE80:0:0:0:1:0:0:200%42]:80. A POSIX local address is just the path string, /var/agentx/master, and a DNS example is www.example.net:80.
sections.eli5: The examples show the same address written two ways: the bytes a computer stores and the neat text a person reads.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The module defines no management objects. It only defines textual conventions that other MIB modules may use. The RFC argues that meaningful security considerations can only be written for modules that define concrete management objects, so this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: This note only designs the address boxes, not anything that holds real data, so there is nothing here to lock up.
